title: Why I'd Vote to Keep the Uniform
paragraphs: Every September, I complain about my school uniform. The skirt is itchy, the tie is pointless, and the colour, a dark green, makes everyone look slightly seasick. Yet if somebody asked me to vote on abolishing it tomorrow, I would vote no. I know that is not a popular opinion among my classmates, so let me explain.

First, uniforms reduce pressure. I have friends who spent twenty minutes every morning worrying about what to wear in their previous schools, and others who felt embarrassed because their clothes were not new. With a uniform, nobody can tell whose family earns more. For a teenager, that is no small thing.

Second, there is the question of identity. When I wear the green jumper, I belong to something larger than my own group of friends. It is the same feeling you get from a football shirt: a sense that you are part of a team. I admit that it sounds sentimental, but I noticed it clearly last year at an inter-school competition, when our students, who rarely agree on anything, cheered together like one big family.

Third, there is a practical argument. Uniforms are usually cheaper in the long run, since you do not need a large wardrobe for school, and they can be passed down from older brothers and sisters. In my school in Guayaquil, a second-hand uniform shop run by parents sells jumpers for five dollars, which is a fraction of the price of a new one.

Of course, there are valid criticisms. Uniforms can be uncomfortable in hot weather, and some students, especially those who do not identify with traditional gender rules, feel restricted by them. The solution, however, is not to abolish uniforms but to improve them: lighter fabric, trousers available for everyone, and a simple version for hot days. Our school, in fact, changed its skirt policy last year after a student petition.

In the end, uniforms are not about control; they are about equality and belonging. If I am honest, I will probably complain again next September. But I will do it wearing my green jumper, and I will be quietly glad that nobody can judge me by my clothes.

title: Before Dawn at the Fish Market
paragraphs: The first trucks arrive at the fish market at two in the morning. By four, the floor is wet, the air smells of salt, and the whole building is a river of shouting voices. Boxes of squid, mackerel and crab are weighed, auctioned and carried away in less than an hour. A stranger might think that nobody is in charge, but every movement here follows a pattern learned over decades.

Haeun Park, twenty-four, has been working at the market in Busan, South Korea, for two years. She started by helping her mother, who sells dried fish from a small stall, and she has now taken over the accounts. 'People think this is a job for old women,' she says, wiping her hands on her apron. 'And, honestly, most of the sellers are. But the old women have been telling me for two years that I count too slowly, and now they're asking me to teach them to use the app.'

The app is Haeun's contribution: a simple program that lets customers in distant cities order fresh fish, which is packed in ice and delivered the same day. Sales have risen steadily since she introduced it, although she is careful not to exaggerate her role. 'My mother's customers have stayed with her for thirty years,' she says. 'The app brings new ones, but it can't replace trust.'

That trust is built in small gestures. A seller will tell you honestly that today's squid is not the best and recommend the mackerel instead, even though it is cheaper. Another will add an extra fish to your bag because it is your birthday. Such habits do not appear on any balance sheet, but they keep people coming back.

The market faces serious challenges, however. Younger people prefer supermarkets, fish stocks are under pressure in many seas, and the building itself needs expensive repairs. Several stalls have already closed in the last decade. Haeun's mother worries about the future, and she tells her daughter that she should find an easier job.

At eight, the noise begins to fade, and the sellers sit down to eat a bowl of hot soup that costs about eight thousand won. Haeun eats beside her mother, checking orders on her phone between each mouthful. 'I don't know if I'll stay forever,' she admits. 'But for now, there's nowhere I'd rather be at six in the morning.'

title: Review: Café Quiet, Cape Town
paragraphs: The first thing you notice about Café Quiet, which opened last spring in a converted warehouse in Cape Town, is what you don't hear. There is no music, no shouting of orders and no phone ringing. A small sign by the door explains the rules: whispering is fine, laptops are welcome, and mobile phones must be placed in a numbered locker.

I went in sceptical, expecting a gimmick. I suspected that the idea would be tiresome after twenty minutes, and that the owner, a former teacher named Thandiwe Mokoena, had invented a clever way to charge people for silence. I was wrong, at least about the first part. Within half an hour, my shoulders had dropped, and I was reading a book I had been carrying around for three months.

The café itself is simple and attractive. Long wooden tables fill the centre, while armchairs occupy the corners for those who prefer to curl up. Light comes through large windows, and the walls are decorated with photographs taken by local students. The menu is short: coffee, tea, a few pastries and one excellent carrot cake, which was moist and not too sweet. A coffee costs forty rand, which is not cheap but is not outrageous either.

Is it perfect? Not quite. The lockers are small, and those who need to take calls for work have to leave the building, which is inconvenient on rainy days. Some customers also find the silence oppressive, especially when sitting alone. I noticed a group of teenagers who left after ten minutes, apparently unable to bear it. The owner says this is fine: 'The café isn't for everybody,' she told me. 'It's for people who are tired.'

That sentence stayed with me. In a city, and a world, where noise is constant, a place that offers calm feels almost radical. I am not suggesting that every café should copy the idea. But I would love to see more spaces where nobody expects you to talk, post or perform.

I will certainly return, probably on a Sunday afternoon, with a book and no particular plan. Take a friend if you like, but be prepared: the best conversations in Café Quiet are the ones you have with yourself. Three and a half stars out of five.

title: Bags with a Second Life: A Young Designer Speaks
paragraphs: Chidera Okafor is twenty-one, studies design in Lagos and runs a small business that turns discarded rice sacks and advertising banners into bags. Her products, which have attracted customers from three continents, sell for between eight and twenty thousand naira. We asked her how it all began.
Q: What was the first bag you made?

A: A disaster. I was nineteen, my sewing machine was my aunt's, and I had never made anything bigger than a cushion. The bag looked like a sack with a handle sewn on. But my sister carried it to university anyway, and three strangers asked where she had bought it. That was the moment I thought: maybe there's something here.
Q: Why use recycled materials?

A: Partly because of money. New fabric was expensive, and an old sack cost almost nothing. But there's also a reason I care about. Lagos produces an enormous amount of waste, and I see a banner thrown away behind a printing shop every day. Giving it a second life makes me feel useful.
Q: What is the hardest part of running the business?

A: Trust. Online customers worry that a bag made from a banner won't be well finished, so I post videos of the entire process, including my mistakes. Funny enough, those videos are more popular than the photos of perfect products. People enjoy seeing that a real person is behind the work.
Q: Have you ever thought of giving up?

A: Last year, definitely. A big order from abroad arrived late because of problems at customs, and the customer asked for a refund. I lost nearly a month's profit. I cried, I slept, and then I asked a friend to help me improve my packaging and delivery. If that hadn't happened, I might have closed the business.
Q: Any advice for people your age?

A: Start before you feel ready. And don't hide your mistakes; people trust honesty more than perfection. Oh, and learn to say no. When you're young, you accept everything, and you end up exhausted. Last Friday I refused a job that would have meant working all night. The world did not end.

title: The Strange Comfort of Rereading
paragraphs: Most people have a book they have read more than once. Strangely, we rarely admit it. Reading a book for the second time feels, to many, like a small failure of ambition: so many unread titles wait on the shelf, so why return to the same one? I would like to argue that rereading is not a waste of time but one of the most rewarding habits a reader can develop.

The first benefit is depth. When you read a story for the first time, you are mainly following the plot, hurrying to discover what happens. You cannot appreciate the details because you do not yet know which ones are important. The second time, free from suspense, you notice the foreshadowing, the small phrases that hint at the ending, and the way the author slowly builds a character. It is rather like visiting a city you already know: you stop looking at the map and start looking at the streets.

The second benefit is that the book changes because you do. I first read a famous novel about a family in a village at sixteen, when I thought the elderly characters were boring. Reading it again at twenty-five, I found them the most interesting people in the story. The words had not changed, of course; I had. A reread is therefore a kind of mirror, showing us how much we have developed in the years between.

There is also comfort. After a stressful week, it can be restful to open a novel in which nothing can surprise you. You already know that the heroine will survive, that the misunderstanding will be cleared up, and that the last page is as satisfying as you remember. Some psychologists suggest that this predictability is precisely what makes the experience soothing, although I confess that I have no scientific evidence beyond my own armchair.

Of course, rereading has limits. Not all books deserve a second visit, and a text that depends entirely on a surprising ending can lose its magic. Besides, time is finite, and no one can reread everything. But I suspect that most readers would benefit from choosing, now and then, an old favourite instead of the latest bestseller.

So the next time you feel guilty about opening a book you already know, remember that you are not going backwards. You are simply walking the same road at a different speed, and noticing what you missed.

title: Seven Minutes
paragraphs: Lucrecia had exactly seven minutes to cross the city, and the city was against her. It was seven fifty-three, and her chemistry exam, the one that would decide whether she could apply for a scholarship, began at eight o'clock sharp. The doors closed at eight, and no one was admitted after that. She was standing in a crowded bus that had not moved for ten minutes, behind a truck that had broken down in the middle of the main road in Quetzaltenango.

She did the only reasonable thing: she got off the bus, took her backpack, and ran. She had less than a kilometre to go, uphill, in school shoes that were not designed for running. Her mother's voice echoed in her head: 'You have studied for six months, mija. Don't let a bus ruin it.'

After four blocks, her lungs were burning. At the corner of the plaza, a boy of about ten, selling chewing gum from a cardboard box, stared at her. 'Exam?' he asked. She nodded, unable to speak. He grinned, put his box on the ground and said, 'Follow me. I know a shortcut.'

Lucrecia hesitated for exactly one second. Then she followed him through a narrow passage between two houses, past a yard where a dog barked and a woman hung out the laundry, and out onto a steep street she had never seen before. 'Straight up,' he said. 'Then left at the blue wall.' She thanked him breathlessly, pressed a ten-quetzal note into his hand and kept running.

She arrived at the school gate at one minute to eight, red-faced and shaking. The security guard looked at his watch, then at her, and smiled. 'Go, go!' he said, opening the gate. She ran along the corridor, found her room, dropped into her seat, and, as the teacher began to hand out the papers, realised that she had forgotten her pencil case.

A girl at the next desk silently slid a pen across the narrow gap between them. Lucrecia whispered a thank-you, took a long breath, and turned over the first page. The questions were difficult, but they were questions she knew. Somewhere in the city, she thought, a bus was still stuck behind a truck, and a boy with a cardboard box was counting his money. She smiled, and began to write.

title: Vegetarian Option Trial: Findings
paragraphs: ## Introduction

The school management asked the Student Council to evaluate whether the canteen could offer a daily vegetarian option. This report presents the findings of a two-week trial and a student survey carried out at Liceo Nuevo Mundo in Santiago, Chile.
## The trial

During the trial, the canteen offered a vegetarian main course, such as lentil stew or vegetable rice, alongside the traditional meat dish. The vegetarian option was priced at 2,300 pesos, the same as the usual dish.
## Findings

On average, 38 of the 210 students who ate at the canteen each day chose the vegetarian option (about 18 per cent). The number rose from 25 in the first week to 51 in the second, probably because students gradually lost their initial suspicion. Opinions about taste were mixed: lentil stew received the best ratings, while the vegetable rice was criticised as bland. In the survey, completed by 150 students, 96 (64 per cent) said they would be willing to try vegetarian food at least once a week, while 54 (36 per cent) said they would not.

The kitchen staff reported that the vegetarian dishes were cheaper to prepare, with ingredients costing about 15 per cent less. However, they also pointed out that preparing two main courses increased the workload and sometimes caused a delay in the serving line, particularly in the first week.
## Recommendations

Because the results were encouraging, we recommend keeping the vegetarian option permanently. To avoid delays, the cooks suggest preparing the vegetarian dish in larger quantities one day in advance, since stews tend to improve after a day. Moreover, a short taste-and-vote event could help the menu to evolve according to student preferences. Finally, the council proposes to repeat the survey at the end of the term to check whether the interest persists.

title: A Letter Applying for an Exchange Programme
paragraphs: Dear Ms Alvarez,

I am writing to apply for a place on the Youth Exchange Programme in Toronto next autumn, as advertised on your website. I am seventeen years old and in my final year at Instituto Central in Tegucigalpa, Honduras, where I have studied English since the age of eight.

I believe I would be a strong candidate for several reasons. Firstly, my academic record is solid: my average mark over the last two years has been 92 per cent, and I received a prize for the best English grade in my year. Secondly, I have experience of working with others. For the last eighteen months, I have volunteered as a tutor at a community library, helping younger children with reading and homework twice a week. Thirdly, I am organised and reliable: I have never missed a tutoring session.

My main motivation for applying is to improve my spoken English in a natural environment. Although I read and write confidently, I have rarely had the opportunity to speak with native speakers, and I sometimes lose confidence in conversation. I have also been reading Canadian authors, and I would like to see the places I have read about. I hope to study environmental science at university, and Toronto's universities have excellent reputations in that field.

I should mention that the cost of the programme, 4,500 Canadian dollars, is beyond my family's means, although they could contribute about a third. I would therefore like to apply for the partial scholarship described in your brochure. I have attached a letter from my school principal and a copy of my latest report.

If I were selected, I would do my best to represent my country and my school with pride. I am aware that living abroad can be difficult; I expect to feel homesick at times, but I am confident I can adapt. I would also be happy to share my experience with other students on my return, perhaps through a short presentation.
Thank you for considering my application. I would welcome the chance to attend an interview, either in person or online, at your convenience.
Yours sincerely,
Renata Arce

title: Banning Teenagers Is Not the Answer
paragraphs: When I was thirteen, I lied about my age to open a social media account. It took me thirty seconds: I selected a different year of birth and clicked 'accept'. That was almost eight years ago, and I am still here, apparently unharmed. I mention this because the debate about banning teenagers from social media usually forgets one fact: young people are remarkably good at finding ways around rules.

Supporters of a ban have good intentions. They point to anxiety, cyberbullying and endless scrolling, and they argue that childhood should be protected. I share their concern. I have friends who spent whole nights comparing themselves with strangers, and I have felt the same discomfort. Nevertheless, I do not think that an age limit is the right answer.

First, enforcement is nearly impossible. To prove a user's age, platforms would need to collect documents or scan faces, which creates new privacy risks for everyone, including adults. Second, a ban can push teenagers toward less regulated corners of the internet, where there are no reporting tools and no adults paying attention. A forbidden platform is not a safe platform; it is merely an invisible one.

Third, and most importantly, social media is not only harmful. For me, it has been the place where I discovered a community of young photographers, found a part-time job, and kept in touch with cousins in another country. Removing these opportunities by law would be like closing a library because it contains some bad books.

What would work better? Education, I believe, combined with better design. Schools could teach students how recommendation algorithms work, how to recognise manipulated images and how to take a break. Companies, in turn, should be obliged to switch off by default the features that encourage endless use, such as automatic playing of the next video and notifications at night.

Parents have a role too, but not as inspectors. A conversation at dinner about what you saw online is worth more than a hundred password checks. Teenagers do not need to be locked out; they need to be taught how to walk through a very noisy room without losing themselves.

questions.explain_es: Dice que una conversación 'is worth more than a hundred password checks'.

questions.q: What can we infer about the author's own experience of social media?
options: It has been entirely negative for the author
It has been entirely positive for the author
It has had both positive and negative effects
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: habla de incomodidad ('the same discomfort') pero también de una comunidad de fotógrafos, un empleo y contacto con primos.

questions.q: Why does the author compare a ban to closing a library?
options: To show that a ban would remove useful things too
To suggest that libraries are dangerous
To argue that books are better than screens
questions.explain_es: Propósito: 'Removing these opportunities by law would be like closing a library because it contains some bad books'.

questions.q: In 'switch off by default', 'by default' means…
options: because the law requires it
because of a technical mistake
automatically, unless changed
questions.explain_es: Las empresas deberían desactivar esas funciones desde el inicio, sin que el usuario deba hacerlo: 'by default' es por defecto.
